lesson.title: Sharing electron pairs

steps.headline: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms.

lead.text: Some atoms are close to a full outer shell and share rather than swap. Both atoms count the shared pair as their own.
In a Lewis drawing each bond line is one shared pair.
Hydrogen, H₂, is drawn with a single line between its atoms.

reveal.text: You turned one line into one pair, and one pair into its electrons. That is all a single bond is.

steps.headline: Carbon dioxide has two double bonds. How many electrons are shared altogether?

workedSteps.text: A double bond is two shared pairs.
Each pair holds two electrons, so count in pairs first and then double.

steps.headline: Oxygen, O₂, has one double bond. How many electrons does it share?

workedSteps.text: A double bond is two shared pairs.

steps.headline: A shared pair counts for both atoms, while a lone pair stays on one atom.

lead.text: Not every outer electron is shared. Electrons that stay on one atom, as a pair, are lone pairs. They are drawn as two dots.
A shared pair is still only one pair in the molecule, even though both atoms count it.
Ethene, C₂H₄, has one double bond between the carbons and four single C–H bonds.
Nitrogen, N₂, is held together by a triple bond.

lesson.orientation: Read single, double and triple bonds and distinguish shared electrons from lone pairs.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two chlorine atoms each have 7 outer electrons. Each puts one electron into a pair that both atoms count as their own.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the shared and unshared electrons in a Lewis drawing.

recap.keyIdea: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons that both atoms count toward their shells. More bond lines mean more shared pairs, and lone pairs stay with one atom.

blocks.text: You counted 4 shared electrons in O₂, 8 across the two double bonds in CO₂ and 12 in ethene. Each time you took pairs first and then doubled.

recap.nextHook: A formula only lists atoms. Next: how to read the subscripts and coefficients in a chemical formula.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the single bond of H₂?
hints: Count two electrons per shared pair.
A single line means one shared pair.
How many electrons make one pair?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One bonding pair contains two electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. One bond line is one shared pair, and a pair is two electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: One electron is only half a pair. Each atom adds one, so the pair holds both.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the double bond of O₂?
hints: Each bond line represents one pair.
A double bond has two shared pairs.
Multiply 2 pairs by 2 electrons per pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two pairs contain four shared electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A double bond is two shared pairs, and each pair holds two electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one pair. A double bond has two pairs.

questions.prompt: How does a shared pair contribute to the two bonded atoms?
hints: Keep shell counting separate from the total electron count.

acceptedIdeas: Each atom counts the pair toward its shell
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A shared pair counts toward both shells while remaining one pair in the molecule.

choices.label: Each atom counts the pair toward its shell
Each atom receives two new extra electrons
Only the heavier atom counts the pair

questions.onCorrect: Both atoms count the same shared pair toward their shells, and it is still one pair in the molecule.

misconceptions.feedback: No new electrons are made. The same pair is counted by both atoms.
Both atoms count the shared pair, not just the heavier one.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared in the triple bond of N₂?
hints: Multiply the number of lines by two.
A triple bond has three shared pairs.
Multiply 3 pairs by 2 electrons per pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three shared pairs contain six electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 6. A triple bond is three shared pairs of two electrons each.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the pairs. The question asks for the electrons.

questions.prompt: NH₃ has one lone pair on nitrogen. How many nonbonding electrons is that?
hints: A lone pair is not a bond line.
The prompt gives one lone pair.
How many electrons make one pair?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A lone pair contains two electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 2. A lone pair is one pair of electrons that stays on a single atom.

misconceptions.feedback: A lone pair is two electrons, because it is a pair.

questions.prompt: Methane is drawn with four bonds on a flat screen. What can you infer from this Lewis drawing?
hints: Read bond connections without treating screen angles as measurements.

acceptedIdeas: It has four single C–H bonds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The diagram records four single bonds; it does not specify the real tetrahedral geometry.

choices.label: Its atoms must all lie in one plane
It has four single C–H bonds
Its bond angles must be 90 degrees

questions.onCorrect: The drawing shows four single C–H bonds. It is a bookkeeping diagram and does not show the real angles.

misconceptions.feedback: A flat drawing does not tell you the atoms lie in one plane.
The screen angles are a drawing choice, not a measurement.

questions.prompt: How many outer electrons does each chlorine atom now count?
hints: Each atom still counts the electron it put into the pair.
It also counts the electron its partner put in.
Add the partner's contribution to the starting count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7 + 1 = 8: each atom counts its own seven plus its partner's one.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Each atom counts both electrons of the shared pair, which fills its outer shell. That is a covalent bond.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before sharing. Each atom now also counts its partner's electron.
That adds both atoms' electrons. Each atom counts only its own shell.

questions.prompt: Ammonia, NH₃, is drawn with three N–H bond lines. How many shared pairs is that?
hints: What does one bond line stand for?
Count the lines.
One pair for each line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each line is one shared pair, and there are three lines.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each bond line is one shared pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts electrons. The question asks for pairs.
Each line is a pair of its own, so count every line.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the number of pairs by 2?

acceptedIdeas: Each shared pair contains two electrons

choices.label: Each shared pair contains two electrons
Each pair is shared by two molecules
A double bond always doubles the atoms

questions.onCorrect: Right: a pair is two electrons, so electrons are twice the number of pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: A pair is shared by two atoms inside one molecule, not two molecules.
Bonds do not change the number of atoms. They count pairs of electrons.

questions.prompt: How many electrons are shared altogether in ethene, C₂H₄?
hints: Count the shared pairs in the double bond first.
Add the four single bonds, one pair each.
Turn the total number of pairs into electrons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The double bond is 2 pairs and the four single bonds are 4 pairs: 6 pairs, so 12 electrons.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Count the pairs in all the bonds, then double.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. Turn it into electrons.
That counts only the double bond. Add the single bonds.
That counts only the four single bonds. Add the double bond.

questions.prompt: Water has two lone pairs on its oxygen atom. How many nonbonding electrons is that?
hints: What is one lone pair made of?
Count the pairs given.
Turn pairs into electrons.
questions.onCorrect: 4. Each lone pair is two unshared electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the pairs. The question asks for the electrons.
